principles.chapter: The Secret Advantages of Option Trading
principles.principle: Options give stock-like leverage with limited risk, so a speculative allocation can be held via options while risking only a small fraction (about 10%) of the portfolio.
principles.quote: you could receive the same kind of leverage by buying options and utilizing option strategies yet only risking 10% of your portfolio

rule.notes: Illustrative: using options instead of high-flying stocks lets you get leverage while risking ~10% of the portfolio; book frames it as an example, not a hard cap (hard caps appear in Secrets 25 and 94).

principles.chapter: The Secret Advantages of Option Trading
principles.principle: Options must be used with prudence; overdosing (overleveraging) is dangerous.
principles.quote: like all miracle drugs, options must be used with prudence and proper care

rule.notes: Qualitative caution against over-allocation.

principles.principle: Get proper option education from active-trader authorities who avoid hype before trading.
principles.quote: To be a successful option trader, you must get the proper education.

rule.notes: Educational prerequisite; not machine-checkable.

principles.principle: Paper trade first, especially before high-risk strategies such as naked writing.
principles.quote: Playing it on paper becomes more important when you are considering high risk trades, such as naked writing.

rule.notes: Before first real naked-writing trade, recommend a paper-trading period. Book also warns not to paper trade too long; real learning requires real money. No duration given.

principles.principle: Do not paper trade too long; real learning only occurs with real money at stake.
principles.quote: don’t paper trade for too long, for real learning only occurs when real money is on the line

rule.notes: No duration specified.

principles.chapter: Stick a Toe in the Water
principles.principle: Beginners should start by buying a small number of options and avoid spreads and option writing.
principles.quote: buying options is the best way to start trading options. Avoid entering spreads or option writing.

rule.notes: For novice users, warn on spreads and writing; recommend small long-option positions first.

principles.chapter: Stick a Toe in the Water
principles.principle: Start with very small positions and never plunge in, no matter how good the situation looks.
principles.quote: no matter how good the situation may look, avoid plunging into the water!

rule.notes: Small initial positions; no numeric limit here.

principles.principle: Do option analysis before entering any strategy and monitor positions properly afterward.
principles.quote: doing option analysis before entering an option strategy and then properly monitoring that position

rule.notes: Require analysis (fair value, probability, delta) before order entry; require ongoing monitoring.

principles.chapter: Those Who Use Crystal Balls Eat Chipped Glass
principles.principle: Assume markets are random rather than trying to predict short-term moves.
principles.quote: the best way to approach the markets is to assume that they are random

rule.notes: Default modeling assumption: random (no drift) market.

principles.chapter: Those Who Use Crystal Balls Eat Chipped Glass
principles.principle: Choose strategies that can profit without being right about direction (high-probability writing or buying where one winner pays for many losers).
principles.quote: you don’t have to be right about the market 50% of the time

rule.notes: Strategy design principle.

principles.chapter: Those Who Use Crystal Balls Eat Chipped Glass
principles.principle: Trester's newsletter used a random approach, always recommending equal numbers of puts and calls (three of each per issue).
principles.quote: We always recommended three puts and three calls for purchase in each issue.

rule.notes: Balanced put/call selection under randomness assumption (later biased toward puts, Secret 34).

principles.principle: An option buyer's probability of winning on any single play is always below 50% in a random market, and much lower for out-of-the-money options.
principles.quote: Your probability of winning when you buy options will always be less than 50% in a random market.

rule.notes: Sanity check: computed probability of profit for a held-to-expiration long option should be <50%; if model shows higher, flag. OTM options lower still.

principles.principle: Expect losing streaks even when doing everything right; stick to the game plan rather than changing methodology.
principles.quote: even if you are doing everything right when you trade options, you could incur a long losing streak

rule.notes: On losing streaks, discourage abandoning the system. If losses are intolerable, shift to higher-probability strategies.

principles.principle: Regression to the mean: cheap/undervalued options tend to become fairly valued or expensive; overvalued options tend to cheapen; quiet markets tend to become volatile.
principles.quote: Options that are cheap and undervalued are likely to become properly valued or expensive, and overvalued options tend to get less expensive.

rule.notes: Supports buying when IV is low vs its history and writing when IV is high vs its history.

principles.principle: After a hot streak, expect regression; be cautious.
principles.quote: If you are on a hot streak, look out!

rule.notes: Behavioral caution.

principles.principle: No guru or system works all the time; use experts' wisdom but make your own decisions.
principles.quote: Use the wisdom of the experts, but make your own decisions

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.principle: Even advanced AI forecasting (neural nets) only predicts index moves about 60% of the time; markets approach randomness and you need not predict.
principles.quote: have formed systems that predict market moves about 60% of the time

rule.notes: Cap assumed predictive accuracy of any forecast model at ~60%.

principles.principle: Be a contrarian at true extremes: buy when fear is extreme, sell when euphoria is extreme; be patient for real extremes.
principles.quote: Buy when there is a lot of fear in the market and sell when there is a lot of euphoria and greed in the market.

rule.notes: Act only at real extremes.

principles.principle: VIX moving above 35% suggests the market is near a bottom (bullish signal), except when the market is genuinely highly volatile, where VIX is less predictive.
principles.quote: The index moving above 35% suggests that we are near a market bottom.

rule.notes: If VIX > 35, flag possible market bottom / favor bullish strategies. Exception: if realized market volatility is itself very high, VIX is less predictive (Secret 11, p.36-37).

principles.principle: Use chart support and resistance when setting stop-losses and profit goals.
principles.quote: I look closely at support and resistance when designing my strategies, especially when setting stop-losses and profit goals.

rule.notes: Place stops/targets relative to support and resistance levels.

principles.principle: Breakouts from tight trading ranges signal a major change in volatility and improved odds of a big move.
principles.quote: I also watch for breakouts from tight trading ranges.

rule.notes: Breakout from narrow range = favorable for option buying.

principles.principle: Give more weight to trends with heavy volume and no supporting news; price below long-term support implies further decline; new highs tend to go higher and new lows lower.
principles.quote: I put much more importance on trends when there is a lot of volume and no news to support the move.

rule.notes: Trend signal weight: high volume + no news = strongest. New high -> likely higher; new low -> likely lower; break of long-term support -> likely continued fall.

principles.principle: Suddenly very expensive/overpriced options on a stock that is not moving suggest an undisclosed news event—be suspicious.
principles.quote: When option premiums on a stock are suddenly very expensive and overpriced even though the stock price is not moving much, you should be suspicious.

rule.notes: Flag IV spike with flat underlying as possible undisclosed event risk (especially for writers).

principles.chapter: Use the Laws of Supply and Demand
principles.principle: For commodities at extreme high/low prices, buy options (limited risk) rather than futures; be patient and roll into new options on expiration until supply/demand reasserts.
principles.quote: Options, because of their limited risk, are ideal for taking a position if a commodity is really high or really low in price.

rule.notes: Prefer long options over futures when betting on mean reversion of commodity extremes.

principles.chapter: Sell in May and Go Away
principles.principle: Seasonality: holding stocks October to start of May produced ~10x the gains of May–September over 50 years; markets tend to decline in May–June and September–October.
principles.quote: holding stocks only from October till the start of May showed 10 times greater gains than holding stocks only from May till September

rule.notes: Bearish seasonal months: May, June, September, October. Use as a bias input only.

principles.chapter: Sell in May and Go Away
principles.principle: The best time to buy stocks is near the end of October (most crashes occurred in October; institutional tax-loss selling).
principles.quote: No question that the best time to buy stocks is near the end of October.

rule.notes: Bullish entry seasonality near end of October; December weak due to individual tax-loss selling.

principles.chapter: Sell in May and Go Away
principles.principle: End-of-month effect: stocks tend to rise on the last trading day of the month and first four trading days of the next (up 70% of the time in bull markets, 50% in bear markets).
principles.quote: Stock prices tend to rise on the last trading day of the month and the first four days of the month.

rule.notes: Bullish window; frequencies 70% (bull) / 50% (bear).

principles.chapter: Sell in May and Go Away
principles.principle: Stocks tend to rise on the day before a holiday.
principles.quote: stock prices tend to rise on the day before a holiday

rule.notes: Bullish bias on pre-holiday session.

principles.chapter: Sell in May and Go Away
principles.principle: Commodity seasonals: corn highs June/July, lows December; soybeans highs May, lows Oct/Nov; wheat highs Dec/Jan, lows May; cattle highs Apr/May, lows July; hogs highs Jun–Aug, lows Nov/Dec.
principles.quote: corn prices (based on weekly nearby futures) tend to make their highs for the year in June or July and make their lows in December

rule.notes: Based on a 10–14 year study of weekly nearby futures.

principles.principle: The 60% Rule: assume you will be right at most 60% of the time regardless of conviction, and design strategies that still pay off at 60% or lower accuracy.
principles.quote: That rule assumes that I will only be right 60% of the time no matter how I feel about a position or projection.

rule.notes: Any user directional conviction must be capped at 60% when computing expected value; reject strategies that are profitable only if directional accuracy > 60%. Stronger conviction should not raise this.

principles.principle: For stock investing, buy a low-fee index fund/ETF (QQQ, SPY) by dollar averaging the same dollars each month, probably in the third week of the month.
principles.quote: putting the same number of dollars in the market each month (probably in the third week of the month)

rule.notes: Core stock allocation via monthly dollar-cost averaging into index ETFs.

principles.principle: The stronger you believe an event will occur, the more likely you are wrong; consensus agreement is a warning sign.
principles.quote: the stronger you think that an event is likely to occur, the more likely that you will be wrong

rule.notes: Contrarian check on high-conviction inputs.

principles.chapter: Predicting Stock Tops and Market Bottoms
principles.principle: Topping signal: after a strong uptrend, extremely high volume for two or three days in a row with no upward price progress indicates a top—take profits on stock or calls (puts become attractive).
principles.quote: My rule of thumb is that the volume must be extremely high for two or three days in a row.

rule.notes: Condition: strong prior uptrend AND extremely high volume for 2–3 consecutive days AND no upward price progress -> take profits on long stock/calls; consider puts. 'Extremely high' not quantified.

principles.chapter: Predicting Stock Tops and Market Bottoms
principles.principle: Market bottoms: when VIX and VNX are at extreme highs (panic), start entering bullish strategies; must be true extremes (e.g. VIX >57% after 9/11).
principles.quote: when the VIX and VNX are extremely high, it is time to start entering bullish strategies

rule.notes: Uses 35% from Secret 11 as the 'near bottom' level; example extreme was VIX >57% (Sept 2001). Bottom may take a few weeks to form.

principles.chapter: Predicting Stock Tops and Market Bottoms
principles.principle: Bottoms form when sellers are exhausted—price stops falling on very high volume.
principles.quote: This occurs when a stock stops dropping in price on very high volume.

rule.notes: Price stalls on very high volume after a decline.

principles.chapter: Get the Biggest Bang for Your Buck
principles.principle: Avoid paying more than 2 ($200) for any stock option or $400 for any futures option, to keep home-run potential.
principles.quote: I set a guideline to avoid paying more than 2 ($200) for any stock option and $400 for any futures option.

rule.notes: Long stock option premium > 2.00 per share ($200/contract) or futures option > $400 -> warn/flag as expensive. (Secret 96 tightens stock options to under 1, LEAPS under 2.5.)

principles.chapter: Get the Biggest Bang for Your Buck
principles.principle: Buying expensive in-the-money options puts a lot at risk and lowers the chance of big percentage gains; cheap options give more bang for the buck.
principles.quote: the higher the price, the smaller the chance of a big percentage gain

rule.notes: Prefer lower-priced options when aiming for high returns.

principles.principle: When you own expensive options, set a stop-loss on the underlying price and sell the option immediately when it is hit.
principles.quote: When you own expensive options, you should have a stop-loss price on the underlying stock or futures price.

rule.notes: Require underlying-based stop for expensive (> guideline price) long options; on trigger, exit immediately.

principles.principle: Cheap options act as an automatic stop-loss: if wrong, you lose only the small premium.
principles.quote: The big advantage of cheap options is that you have an automatic stop-loss.

rule.notes: Cheap long options may forgo explicit stops.

principles.principle: Buy options that are both cheap and undervalued (below theoretical value); most cheap options are overpriced or worthless.
principles.quote: The vast majority of cheap options are overpriced or really worthless.

rule.notes: Long option must be priced below model fair value (price/fair_value < 1) in addition to being cheap.

principles.principle: With truly undervalued options the risk-reward is so good you can win while right only ~30% of the time (Trester's record: 20% winners, 1500% returns in two years).
principles.quote: even if you are right only 30% of the time, you will be a winner

rule.notes: Expected win rate for bargain-option buying can be low (20–30%); evaluate by expected value not win rate.

principles.principle: As an option buyer, aim for home runs (500%–1000% returns); nickel-and-dime profits cannot offset the many losers.
principles.quote: Home runs are best defined as options that return 500% to 1000% returns.

rule.notes: Profit-target design for long cheap options: let part ride toward 500–1000%.

principles.principle: Take profits on half of any long option position when the option doubles in price, and let the rest ride.
principles.quote: My rule here is to take profits on half of any position when your option doubles in price, and let the rest ride!

rule.notes: When option price >= 2x entry, sell 50% of contracts; hold remainder with trailing stop.

principles.principle: Once you have a good paper profit, set a trailing stop on the underlying about 5% away (e.g. stock 50 -> stop 47.5) and exit the rest when hit.
principles.quote: A 5% stop-loss is a good rule of thumb.

rule.notes: For profitable long options: trailing stop on underlying at 5% from current price (below for calls, above for puts); ratchet as underlying moves favorably; exit remainder on touch.

principles.principle: Tighter stops may be appropriate; also exit even without a stop hit when the underlying flattens out or hits resistance/support.
principles.quote: you may still exit a position if you think the underlying stock or futures is flattening out and when you believe it has hit some resistance or support

rule.notes: Discretionary exit trigger: stalling or reaching chart resistance (calls)/support (puts).

principles.principle: Act quickly when things turn against you; with options you usually get only one chance to get out.
principles.quote: If you hesitate, you are lost !

rule.notes: Execute exits promptly; no delay.

principles.principle: Buy enough time: cheap, long-term options with strike near the underlying price are the best buys.
principles.quote: Cheap, long term options, where the strike price is in range of the underlying stock or futures price, are true gems in the rough.

rule.notes: Prefer longer-dated, near-the-money, cheap options. No minimum DTE given here (see Secret 24 and 96).

principles.principle: Always set a time limit on holding an option; for expensive and in-the-money options use a three-week holding period, then exit.
principles.quote: With more expensive options and in-the-money options, I usually set a three week hold period.

rule.notes: For expensive or ITM long options: exit after 21 calendar days if nothing has happened. For others, set some time stop (unspecified).

principles.principle: Avoid holding long options in their last month before expiration, when they depreciate fastest; exit before the last month unless there's little premium left to salvage.
principles.quote: As a general rule, I avoid holding options in their last month before expiration.

rule.notes: Block new long options with < ~1 month (≈30 days) to expiration and exit existing longs before the last month. Exceptions: see OTS-024-b and Secret 39.

principles.principle: Exception: buying options with one month or less left is acceptable if they are extremely cheap and undervalued and the underlying is close to the strike.
principles.quote: sometimes I buy options with one month or less before expiration if they are extremely cheap and undervalued and if the underlying stock or futures price is close to the strike price

rule.notes: Allow last-month long purchase only if: price extremely cheap AND below fair value AND underlying near strike.

principles.principle: Write options a day or two before the last month begins (i.e., around the prior month's expiration).
principles.quote: I write options a day or two before the last month begins (expiration of the previous month).

rule.notes: Writer entry timing: when option enters its final month (~30 DTE or less).

principles.principle: Never take a huge position: any single option position must be less than 5% of the total option-buying portfolio.
principles.quote: Make sure any option position is less than 5% of your total option buying portfolio.

rule.notes: Max cost of any single long option position < 5% of the option-buying capital.

principles.principle: Scale into positions in small steps, adding as the underlying moves while still getting good value; if a super bargain appears, skip scaling and take what you can get.
principles.quote: initially take a small position and then add to it as the underlying moves in price

rule.notes: Staged entry; exception for super bargains.

principles.principle: Scale out: sell some when the option doubles, more when it triples, and so on, leaving a few for a spectacular move.
principles.quote: Sell a few options when they double in price, sell some more when they triple in price and so on

rule.notes: Exit tranches at 2x, 3x (and higher multiples) of cost; keep a small remainder.

principles.principle: Buy at least three options per position so scaling out is possible.
principles.quote: Try to buy at least three options to each position you take.

rule.notes: Minimum 3 contracts per long-option position.

principles.principle: Keep realistic expectations: the goal is a profit each year; unrealistic goals cause excess risk-taking and quitting.
principles.quote: Your goal should be to make a profit, period, each year

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.principle: Never plunge everything into one 'sure thing'; spread purchases over time and positions.
principles.quote: Spread out your purchases over time and position, and never bet everything on that sure thing.

rule.notes: Concentration check; see Secret 25 for numeric cap.

principles.principle: Before buying, compare candidate options on fair price, probability of profit and delta; buy below fair price, prefer higher probability and higher delta; if none is good, pass or trade the underlying.
principles.quote: 1. The fair price of an option 2. The probability of profit 3. The delta

rule.notes: Rank long-option candidates: price < fair value (required), higher P(profit) better, higher delta better. If no candidate qualifies, pass.

principles.principle: Avoid buying options whose strike the underlying is unlikely to reach meaningfully (e.g. a 20 call at 1 with stock at 13 expired worthless even when stock reached 20).
principles.quote: Options have their own risk-reward picture, and you must understand that picture before entering a position.

rule.notes: Compute breakeven (strike + premium) and confirm forecast move exceeds it.

principles.principle: Profit Box: define a price range for the underlying; stay in while it remains in the box and exit immediately if it leaves; maximum holding period of three weeks.
principles.quote: you are only in the position for a maximum of three weeks and you have a very tight stop-loss

rule.notes: For ATM/ITM (high-delta, expensive) buys: exit if underlying leaves predefined box or after 21 days.

principles.principle: Only enter straddles where a simulation shows an 80% or better probability of hitting a profit point during the life of the trade; prefer cheap straddles with plenty of time on historically volatile stocks.
principles.quote: only enter such trades where you have an 80% or better probability of profit

rule.notes: Straddle entry requires simulated probability >= 80% of reaching breakeven/profit at some time before expiration (path-dependent, not at-expiration). Breakevens = strike ± total premium.

principles.principle: Generally avoid straddles because they are expensive and lose if the underlying doesn't move—unless cheap with plenty of time.
principles.quote: if you can find a cheap straddle with plenty of time, you could find a strategy with a high probability of generating a profit

rule.notes: Expensive straddles discouraged.

principles.principle: When a straddle is profitable, scale out and use tight trailing stops; after profiting on one side, consider selling the other side if premium remains.
principles.quote: when you take profits on one side of the position, you may wish to sell the other side if there is some option premium left

rule.notes: Apply Secret 21/22/25 exit rules to straddles.

principles.principle: Be patient: wait for trades with a good risk-reward picture and wait for the profits.
principles.quote: You need the patience to find an option play with a good risk-reward picture, and then you need the patience to wait for the profits!

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.chapter: The Option Buyer's Secret Weapon—Shock and Awe
principles.principle: Real price distributions have fat tails (moves up to 10 standard deviations), so the lognormal Black-Scholes model undervalues options—especially far out-of-the-money ones—giving buyers an edge from surprise volatility.
principles.quote: the pricing model is undervaluing the options, especially the out-of-the-money ones at the ends of the curve

rule.notes: Valuation note: treat lognormal model values of deep OTM options as understated; surprise volatility favors buyers and hurts naked writers.

principles.chapter: The Option Buyer's Secret Weapon—Shock and Awe
principles.principle: Buy options on underlyings with the greatest potential for surprise volatility (tech, hyped/overvalued stocks, single-drug pharma awaiting FDA, industries in flux).
principles.quote: buy options on stocks that have the greatest potential for surprise volatility

rule.notes: Candidate screen: favor event-prone, high-volatility stocks for long options.

principles.principle: Prefer buying options on individual stocks over indexes or futures because stocks have the most surprise volatility (some exceed 100% historical volatility).
principles.quote: there is a big advantage to buying options on stocks rather than other instruments, such as futures

rule.notes: Long-option candidate preference: stock > index/futures.

principles.principle: Bias the option-buying portfolio with more puts than calls: puts produced the best returns and most home runs, stocks fall faster than they rise, and puts are usually cheaper.
principles.quote: I would bias my options portfolio with more puts than calls.

rule.notes: Long-option portfolio should hold more puts than calls (count or dollars); always hold both.

principles.principle: Diversify option buying across many positions, both puts and calls; few positions can wipe out the portfolio.
principles.quote: the more positions you have increases your odds of hitting a home run

rule.notes: Warn when the long-option book is concentrated in few positions or only one side (calls only / puts only).

principles.principle: Diversify over time: don't buy many positions at once; enter gradually and keep reserves, increasing buying when the market wakes up.
principles.quote: Don’t buy a lot of option positions at one time.

rule.notes: Spread entries over time; maintain cash reserve for losing streaks. No numeric limit given (Secret 96 says diversify over 2 years).

principles.principle: Budget a set dollar amount for option buying each year and invest it gradually over the year, possibly using seasonal tendencies.
principles.quote: plan to spend a set amount of dollars each year and gradually to invest that capital over that period

rule.notes: Track annual option-buying budget and pacing.

principles.principle: Option buying requires close surveillance and quick action; inertia (fear of loss, slowness to take profit) is the buyer's greatest enemy.
principles.quote: Inertia is the greatest enemy of the option buyer.

rule.notes: Monitor long positions frequently; act on triggers immediately.

principles.principle: Always hold some puts to insure a stock/mutual-fund portfolio against unexpected declines.
principles.quote: always to hold some puts in their portfolio in order to protect their stock positions and mutual funds from unexpected market declines

rule.notes: If user holds equities, recommend a small put insurance sleeve.

principles.principle: Don't over-insure: buy cheap out-of-the-money puts as a safety net costing only a very small percentage of the portfolio (deductible-style protection).
principles.quote: your put insurance will not be a big investment, just a very small percentage of your portfolio

rule.notes: Cheap OTM puts, small % of portfolio. Exact % not given (see 5–10% speculative cap in Secret 94).

principles.principle: Insurance puts should still be undervalued with decent probability of profit and delta; they need not be on the stocks you own, so be a bargain hunter.
principles.quote: make sure they are undervalued and have a decent probability of profit and delta

rule.notes: Apply long-option value screen to hedge puts too.

principles.principle: In severe declines you sometimes get a second chance to buy puts at reasonable prices on stocks that haven't fallen yet—act quickly.
principles.quote: sometimes you are given a second chance to buy some put insurance

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.chapter: The Second Secret to Portfolio Insurance
principles.principle: Structured products (e.g. principal-guaranteed index notes) give index exposure with built-in downside insurance at the cost of slightly smaller gains; read the prospectus.
principles.quote: Before purchasing shares in one of these structured instruments, do your homework.

rule.notes: Alternative insurance; outside options tool scope.

principles.principle: Long-shot expiration play: in the last week before expiration, buy very close-to-the-money index options (OEX, SPX) priced under 1, on weakness in the option price.
principles.quote: Try to buy options under 1 that are very close to the strike price.

rule.notes: Speculative exception to Secret 24: DTE <= ~7 (last week), index options preferred, price < 1.00, underlying very close to strike, buy on option weakness. Expect many losses; consider paper-trading first; take fast profits.

principles.principle: With expiring-option long shots, act fast on profits (example: bought at 1/8 and immediately placed sell at 1).
principles.quote: The lesson is that fast action is needed with this strategy.

rule.notes: Pre-place profit-taking orders on expiring long shots.

principles.chapter: Take the Bet Instead of Making the Bet
principles.principle: To be a professional option trader you must do some option writing because it provides consistent income; writers can close the position any time by buying back.
principles.quote: to be a professional option trader, you must do some option writing because it provides a consistent source of income

rule.notes: Strategy mix guideline.

principles.chapter: The Secret Advantage of Option Writing
principles.principle: Writing offers very high win probability (sometimes 99%); the writer only gets hurt by a big quick adverse move, but faces unlimited risk.
principles.quote: The only time the option writer gets hurt is when the underlying instrument makes a big quick move against you.

rule.notes: Risk disclosure for naked writing.

principles.principle: Write short-term options with high probability of profit for quick income, remembering the chance of financial ruin.
principles.quote: Writing short term options that have a high probability of profit can generate a lot of income for your portfolio quickly.

rule.notes: See Secret 45 for numeric DTE.

principles.principle: Naked writing has unlimited/extreme risk, especially in crashes; only write naked in an ideal situation and stay defensive.
principles.quote: When at times I write naked puts and calls for speculation, I wait until I find an ideal situation.

rule.notes: Naked writes require all ideal conditions (high probability, short time, overvalued, stop-loss, small size).

principles.chapter: Probability—the First Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: Only write naked options when the probability of success exceeds 90%, found by writing far out-of-the-money options.
principles.quote: Whenever the probability of success is greater than 90%, I have a potential play.

rule.notes: Naked short option: require P(success) > 90% (probability the option expires worthless / stop not hit). Typically requires far OTM strike.

principles.chapter: Probability—the First Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: Always use a stop-loss (based on the underlying) when writing naked; use a simulator to estimate probability of hitting the stop during the option's life.
principles.quote: Whenever you write naked options, you must use a stop-loss to survive.

rule.notes: Naked writes must have an underlying-price stop; compute P(touch stop) via simulation.

principles.chapter: Probability—the First Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: When an option is extremely overpriced or underpriced there is probably a reason—investigate (e.g. pending FDA review, takeover).
principles.quote: When an option is extremely overpriced or extremely underpriced, there is probably a reason.

rule.notes: Flag extreme mispricings for event review before trading.

principles.chapter: Probability—the First Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: OTM writers have time and distance on their side: the underlying must move far enough and fast enough to hit the stop or strike before expiration.
principles.quote: the underlying price must move against them fast enough to beat the expiration date and far enough to hit their stop-loss or strike price

rule.notes: Conceptual basis for short-DTE, far-OTM writing.

principles.chapter: Time—the Second Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: Write options with less than one month to expiration and avoid writing options with more than two months to expiration.
principles.quote: For the writer, write options that have less than one month before expiration.

rule.notes: Preferred writer DTE < ~30 days (one month).

principles.chapter: Time—the Second Secret for Option Writers
principles.principle: Avoid writing options with more than two months before expiration.
principles.quote: Avoid writing options that have more than two months before expiration.

rule.notes: Block/strongly warn on short options (naked writes) with DTE > ~60 days (two months). Exceptions in book: covered call/LEAPS ratio examples and long-term blue-chip put writing to acquire stock (Secret 53).

principles.chapter: Get Out of the Hot Seat!
principles.principle: Get out of the hot seat: buy back written options (naked or high-risk credit spreads) as soon as most of the premium has been captured.
principles.quote: When you are writing naked options or high risk credit spreads and when most of the premium has been captured or disappeared, you MUST EXIT your position.

rule.notes: Exit short when 'most' of the premium is gone. Book gives no exact %; implement as configurable (e.g. user-defined) and cite as 'most of the premium'.

principles.chapter: Get Out of the Hot Seat!
principles.principle: Exit immediately on a major change in the underlying or overall market that you didn't plan for, even if the stop hasn't been hit.
principles.quote: if I see a major change in markets or the underlying security where it is moving against my position in a scenario I didn’t plan for, I will exit immediately

rule.notes: Discretionary exit trigger.

principles.chapter: Get Out of the Hot Seat!
principles.principle: The hot-seat concept also applies to a big profit on a long option: when the underlying stalls or reverses, take the money and run.
principles.quote: When the underlying stock or futures stalls or reverses trend, get out of the the hot seat.

rule.notes: Exit trigger for profitable longs.

principles.principle: Expiration writing: write comfortably out-of-the-money options expiring in just a few days, placing limit sell orders above the current bid, entering many orders in the last two or three days.
principles.quote: put in a lot of orders in the last two or three days before expiration

rule.notes: Expiration-writing setup: DTE 1–3 trading days, strike comfortably OTM, limit price above bid (e.g., bid .3 ask .8, sell at .40). Still subject to surprise volatility.

principles.principle: Ten defensive steps for writers: use stops; only high-probability trades; only short-term options; only overvalued options; cover when most value is lost; never fear a loss; small positions; exit when uncomfortable; exit when the scenario/trend changes; diversify.
principles.quote: Here are ten defensive steps that I take to protect my portfolio from a disastrous hit

rule.notes: Checklist gate for any short-option trade.

principles.principle: The two most important writer defenses are using a stop-loss and taking small positions.
principles.quote: The two most important steps to follow are the use of a stop-loss and taking small positions.

rule.notes: Hard requirements for writers; small size not quantified.

principles.principle: Only write overvalued options (market price above fair value).
principles.quote: 4. Write only overvalued options.

rule.notes: Short option price must exceed model fair value.

principles.principle: Always consider the worst-case scenario when writing: what's the worst that can happen, can I handle it?
principles.quote: Always ask yourself, “What is the worst thing that can happen to the position? Can I handle it? What can go wrong?”

rule.notes: Compute and display worst-case loss (e.g., gap/crash scenario) before a write.

principles.chapter: When to Use Covered Call Writing
principles.principle: Covered call writing is ideal when you have a target sale price for the stock—write calls at that strike and get paid while waiting.
principles.quote: Covered call writing is ideal when you have a target where you wish to sell the stock.

rule.notes: Covered call strike = user's target sale price.

principles.chapter: When to Use Covered Call Writing
principles.principle: If you don't want to sell the stock, only write OTM calls with high probability of expiring, set a stop and buy back if hit, then roll further OTM if desired.
principles.quote: Only write an out-of-the-money option with a high probability of expiring, set a stop-loss and buy back the option if the stop is hit.

rule.notes: OTM strike + underlying stop + buy back on stop + optional roll.

principles.chapter: When to Use Covered Call Writing
principles.principle: Always close covered call positions when most of the premium vanishes; avoid covered calls on stocks in strong uptrends unless a top is expected (then consider selling the stock).
principles.quote: Avoid covered call writing on a stock in a strong up-trend unless you believe it is making a top

rule.notes: Warn on covered calls against strong uptrend; exit when most premium gone.

principles.chapter: The Hidden Risk of Covered Call Writing
principles.principle: Covered calls cap upside yet keep all downside; roll out if the stock crosses the strike, with the stop set very close to the strike.
principles.quote: Your stop-loss should always be set very close to the strike price.

rule.notes: Covered call stop on underlying very near the call strike; roll if crossed.

principles.chapter: The Hidden Risk of Covered Call Writing
principles.principle: Covered calls don't protect the downside (only a point or two); if the stock looks vulnerable, sell it or use a collar instead.
principles.quote: If your stock position looks vulnerable, sell the stock or do a collar (sell a call and buy a put); don’t write covered calls.

rule.notes: When bearish on held stock: recommend sale or collar, not covered call.

principles.principle: Covered call writing on low-priced stocks (under $15) can yield much higher premiums relative to price—but only on stocks you want to own.
principles.quote: write calls on low priced stocks, priced under $15 a share

rule.notes: Higher premium-yield covered calls on stocks < $15; require user wants to own the stock.

principles.chapter: Use Naked Put Writing to Buy Stock
principles.principle: Only write naked puts on stocks you don't mind owning at the strike, and ensure you have enough capital to buy the stock.
principles.quote: I only write puts on stocks that I don’t mind owning at the strike price.

rule.notes: Require cash/buying power >= strike × 100 × contracts and user flag 'willing to own'.

principles.chapter: Use Naked Put Writing to Buy Stock
principles.principle: For naked put writing to acquire stock, use mental stops so a gap below the strike lets you take the stock instead of buying back the put at a big loss.
principles.quote: when I write naked puts, I only use mental stops

rule.notes: For acquisition-intent puts, stop is advisory (alert) rather than a resting order.

principles.chapter: Naked Put Writing Can Create a Win-Win Strategy
principles.principle: Put writing is a win-win way to buy stock lower (net cost = strike − premium), but not appropriate when you want to buy immediately for a pending move.
principles.quote: Put writing is not appropriate when you want to buy a stock right away to take advantage of an immediate pending move.

rule.notes: Show effective cost basis; suggest outright buy if user wants immediate exposure.

principles.chapter: Naked Put Writing Can Create a Win-Win Strategy
principles.principle: Takeover targets often have overvalued puts (arbitrage); write puts only at strikes with long-term chart support.
principles.quote: I only write puts on such stocks at strike prices at a point where they have long term support in the charts.

rule.notes: Put strike at or below long-term support.

principles.chapter: Naked Put Writing Can Create a Win-Win Strategy
principles.principle: Alternative: write longer-term, way out-of-the-money puts on blue-chip stocks you love—either keep the premium or get the stock much cheaper.
principles.quote: he is writing longer term puts. These puts are way out-of-the-money on blue chip stocks that he loves

rule.notes: Exception to short-DTE writer rule for acquisition-intent puts on blue chips.

principles.principle: Options can be valued mathematically (Black-Scholes, based on cost of holding the underlying); the goal is to identify under/overpriced options and pounce.
principles.quote: Your goal is mathematically to identify underpriced or overpriced situations and to pounce on such opportunities.

rule.notes: Compute theoretical value for every option considered.

principles.principle: Pre-trade checklist: (1) fair value—buy undervalued, sell overvalued; (2) probability of profit held to expiration; (3) probability of hitting stop or profit goal during life (simulator); (4) delta—buyers want higher, writers lower.
principles.quote: Make sure you buy undervalued and sell overvalued.

rule.notes: All four metrics computed and displayed for every candidate.

principles.principle: If you cannot get a statistical advantage (under/overvalued or good risk-reward), pass on the trade.
principles.quote: If you cannot get that advantage, pass on the trade.

rule.notes: No-edge trades blocked.

principles.principle: Volatility of the underlying is the key unknown input for fair value and probability; historical (statistical) volatility is the standard deviation of price changes over a set period.
principles.quote: The historical volatility or statistical volatility is a standard deviation of change in price over a set period of days and weeks.

rule.notes: Compute HV as annualized std dev of log price changes.

principles.principle: Match the volatility lookback to holding period: floor traders use 20–30 days; for longer holds use a longer-term historical volatility such as 100 days or 20 weeks.
principles.quote: you should use a longer term historical volatility (i.e. 100 days or 20 weeks)

rule.notes: Default HV lookback for retail holding periods: 100 trading days (or 20 weeks); 20–30 days only for very short-term trading.

principles.principle: Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the model price equal the market price; IV close to historical volatility suggests the option is fairly valued.
principles.quote: the implied volatility will usually come close to matching the historical volatility, suggesting the option is fairly valued

rule.notes: Solve for IV iteratively; compare IV to HV: IV>HV overvalued, IV<HV undervalued.

principles.principle: When IV is extremely low relative to its own history the option is underpriced; extremely high relative to history, overpriced. Same can be done with a historical-volatility chart.
principles.quote: When the implied volatility is extremely low, based on its past history, the underlying option is underpriced.

rule.notes: Buy when IV near historical lows (low IV percentile); write when near highs. Book gives no percentile cutoff ('extremely').

principles.principle: Implied volatility can also be used as the volatility input when calculating probability of profit or running a simulator.
principles.quote: implied volatility can be used when calculating a probability of profit or or when using a simulator

rule.notes: Allow either HV or IV as probability-model input.

principles.chapter: Keep Your Eyes on the Delta
principles.principle: Focus on delta and avoid getting lost in other Greeks (gamma, theta, vega).
principles.quote: it is best to concentrate on the delta and avoid getting lost in the statistics of the other Greeks

rule.notes: Primary Greek in UI = delta.

principles.chapter: Keep Your Eyes on the Delta
principles.principle: Higher delta is better for option buyers; lower delta is better for option writers.
principles.quote: the higher the delta, the better the play for the option buyer; the lower the delta, the better the play for the option writer

rule.notes: Ranking: longs by higher |delta| (among undervalued choices), shorts by lower |delta|.

principles.principle: Compute probability of profit if held to expiration in a random market; best for comparing positions and for spreads held to expiration.
principles.quote: The probability calculator enables you to determine the probability of making a profit if you hold the option positions until expiration in a random market.

rule.notes: Lognormal, zero-bias P(underlying beyond breakeven at expiration).

principles.principle: Option buyers' probability is never greater than 50% in a random market, so buyers must be active and act before expiration.
principles.quote: your probability will never be greater than 50% in a random market

rule.notes: See OTS-007-a.

principles.chapter: The Secret Weapon of Option Analysis
principles.principle: Use simulation (Monte Carlo) to estimate the probability of hitting a profit goal or stop-loss on the underlying during the life of the option.
principles.quote: Simulation enables you to determine the probability of hitting a profit goal or stop-loss price based on the underlying security or futures.

rule.notes: Path simulation of underlying (random walk, lognormal); stops/targets defined on underlying price.

principles.chapter: The Secret Weapon of Option Analysis
principles.principle: Avoid adding a bullish/bearish bias to simulations, or use only a small bias.
principles.quote: Personally I would avoid that feature or enter a small bias

rule.notes: Default drift 0; allow only small bias; warn if user enters a large bias.

principles.chapter: The Secret Weapon of Option Analysis
principles.principle: Simulation forces a game plan with profit goals and stops before entry; if the simulator's prediction doesn't look good, pass.
principles.quote: If the prediction from the simulator doesn’t look good, pass on the trade.

rule.notes: Require profit target and stop before entry; block if simulated outcome poor.

principles.principle: Percent-to-Double: the % move in the underlying needed for the option to double; smaller is better for buyers (reverse for writers); use only for short-term options.
principles.quote: the Percent to Double feature is a tool that should only be used for short term options

rule.notes: Compute required underlying move for 2x option value (short-term options only); rank ascending for buyers.

principles.principle: Use scanners to find under/overvalued plays, but vet results; extremely undervalued options often reflect a preset takeover price, and extremely overpriced ones may signal someone knows something.
principles.quote: when options are extremely overvalued or undervalued, you must question why!

rule.notes: Flag extreme scanner outliers (possible takeover/news).

principles.principle: Situational analysis: all pieces must be in place—likely direction for the time span, overpriced options, high probability of winning (e.g., ~5% chance of hitting stop), and a supportive chart; act immediately on news; take small positions when writing naked.
principles.quote: When you find such a good statistical play, pounce on it, but don’t plunge.

rule.notes: Example: naked call with stop above resistance had 5% simulated stop-hit probability.

principles.chapter: Unraveling the Mysteries of Baysian Analysis
principles.principle: Bayesian decision rule: assign subjective probabilities to price outcomes at expiration, multiply each by the P/L at that price, and sum to get Expected Value; prefer positive EV, recognizing thin EVs.
principles.quote: The result of this multiplication and addition process is called our Expected Value

rule.notes: EV = Σ p_i × PL_i over scenarios. Example: IBM Jul 60 call at 3: 10%→+700, 20%→+200, 40%→0, 30%→−300 ⇒ EV +$20 per $300 risked (thin). Subjective probabilities should be capped per the 60% rule and can be replaced by probability calculator/simulator outputs.

principles.chapter: Unraveling the Mysteries of Baysian Analysis
principles.principle: Be realistic about subjective probabilities; don't let emotion or enthusiasm cloud judgment.
principles.quote: not let emotion and enthusiasm for the stock or futures cloud your judgment

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.principle: Keep analysis software simple: if you can't learn it in 60 minutes, don't use it.
principles.quote: if you can’t learn how to use the software in 60 minutes, don’t use it

rule.notes: UX design principle for the tool itself.

principles.chapter: Your Crystal Ball to the Future or Risk-Reward Analysis Using AI
principles.principle: AI tools can rate a trade by creating an automatic game plan and computing risk-reward and Bayesian expected value.
principles.quote: AI makes options analysis easy for the option trader by giving him or her a method to rate the play, plus Expected Value generated by Baysian Analysis

rule.notes: Auto game plan + rating + EV.

principles.principle: Spreads limit risk and can be designed with high probability of profit; for writers they remove the unlimited risk of naked writing; for buyers they trade home runs for singles and doubles.
principles.quote: For the option writer, spreads can remove the unlimited risk present with naked writing.

rule.notes: Prefer defined-risk spreads over naked writes.

principles.chapter: The Secret Costs of Option Spreads—Beware of Slippage
principles.principle: Minimize trading: spreads magnify commissions and slippage (four trades for a simple spread); keep it simple.
principles.quote: One of my major rules of successful option trading is to minimize your trading.

rule.notes: Display total transaction costs (commission + bid/ask slippage across all legs, in and out).

principles.principle: Avoid alligator spreads—any spread needing three trades to enter (e.g., butterflies)—because commissions and slippage eat you alive.
principles.quote: Avoid any spread that involves three trades to get in the position

rule.notes: Block strategies with 3 or more entry legs (butterflies, condors, etc.).

principles.principle: Avoid delta-neutral strategies that require frequently adding/removing legs.
principles.quote: On paper this strategy looks great, but in practice it rarely works well.

rule.notes: Do not recommend dynamic delta-hedged strategies.

principles.principle: Avoid repair strategies; when a trade goes bad, cut your losses instead of adding legs.
principles.quote: when your option trade goes astray, cut your losses! Don’t use a repair strategy.

rule.notes: On losing positions, recommend closing rather than adding legs.

principles.chapter: How to Reduce the Cost of Option Buying
principles.principle: Debit spreads (vertical or calendar) reduce the cost of buying options but cap profits (no home runs).
principles.quote: Vertical spreads work well for reducing the cost of the position but limit your profits so that you can’t hit home runs.

rule.notes: Trade-off note.

principles.chapter: How to Reduce the Cost of Option Buying
principles.principle: Vertical debit spreads work best when the option bought has lower implied volatility than the OTM option sold (e.g., buy at 30% IV, sell at 40% IV).
principles.quote: if the implied volatility of the option you are purchasing is 30%, but the out-of-the-money option you are writing has an implied volatility of 40%, you have a good play

rule.notes: Favor verticals where IV(short leg) > IV(long leg); example spread of 10 vol points. Also run probability analysis. Max loss = debit (= margin).

principles.principle: Stock/index debit spread design: buy close-to-the-money, sell further OTM; maximum profit must be at least 200%.
principles.quote: 3. The maximum profit must be at least 200%.

rule.notes: Stock/index debit spreads: (width − debit)/debit ≥ 2.0.

principles.principle: Stock/index debit spread: do not sell an option for less than .4.
principles.quote: 4. Do not sell an option for less than .4.

rule.notes: Short leg price ≥ 0.40 for stock/index debit spreads.

principles.principle: Stock/index debit spread: try for probability of profit of 35% or better.
principles.quote: Try to design a spread with a probability of profit of 35% or better.

rule.notes: Debit spread P(profit at expiration) ≥ 35%.

principles.principle: Debit spread long leg should be close-to-the-money and short leg further out-of-the-money.
principles.quote: 1. Buy a close-to-the-money option. 2. Sell a further out-of-the-money option.

rule.notes: Structure check.

principles.principle: Commodity debit spreads: short leg more than one strike out, max profit at least 300%, don't sell an option for less than $100, always use a spread order, probability of profit 35%+, commission no more than $20 round trip per side.
principles.quote: 3. The maximum profit must be at least 300%.

rule.notes: Applies to futures/commodity option debit spreads.

principles.principle: Trade online for faster execution, instant feedback and better prices.
principles.quote: the internet will give you an edge in the market by giving you better trade executions

rule.notes: Execution channel.

principles.principle: Slippage (bid-ask spread) is the hidden cost of trading and can be ~30% of an option's price (e.g., 1 bid / 1.3 ask); reduce trades and trade liquid options with tighter spreads; cheap options have proportionally higher slippage.
principles.quote: try to trade options with more liquidity, options with good volume that trade more often

rule.notes: Compute (ask−bid)/price; book example 30% is presented as a cost to avoid, no explicit cutoff. Prefer higher volume/open interest.

principles.principle: Commissions: paying more than $5 per option means real trouble; try not to pay more than $3 per option.
principles.quote: If you are paying more than $5 per option in commissions, you are in real trouble. Try to avoid paying more than $3 per option.

rule.notes: Commission per contract > $3 warn; > $5 strong warning.

principles.principle: Act like a market maker: public limit orders at the bid have priority over market makers, so you can capture slippage with patient limit orders.
principles.quote: As a public player, you have priority over the market makers’ bid and asked prices.

rule.notes: Default to limit orders; consider buying at the bid / selling at the ask.

principles.chapter: Test the Waters—How to Get the Best Price
principles.principle: Test the waters: place a limit order between bid and ask (e.g., 1.15 on a 1–1.3 market); if unfilled after a few minutes, move to the ask.
principles.quote: Enter a limit price of 1.15 and see if the market maker will bite.

rule.notes: Order workflow: start at/near midpoint, wait a few minutes, then step to ask (buys) or bid (sells).

principles.chapter: You Can Buy the World for 1/8
principles.principle: Don't chase, but be willing to pay an extra .10–.15 to enter a really good opportunity; when you must exit (especially naked writes) try a minute or two then pay what the market bears.
principles.quote: be willing to pay an extra .10 ($10) or .15 ($15) to enter a trade if you have a really good opportunity

rule.notes: Allow up to $0.10–$0.15 concession on good entries; for forced naked-write exits, give 1–2 minutes then market.

principles.principle: Enter spreads with spread limit orders specifying the net debit/credit, avoiding loss of control when legging.
principles.quote: You should usually use spread limit orders to enter spread positions.

rule.notes: Default spread orders as net-price limit orders.

principles.principle: If legging into a spread, enter the long (buy) leg first so you are never naked, and avoid legging in fast-moving markets.
principles.quote: Usually you enter the buy side of the trade first so you are not naked at any time.

rule.notes: Never leg in short first; disallow legging in fast markets; spread orders must be limit orders.

principles.chapter: Don't Tip Your Hand—Beware of Size
principles.principle: Don't tip your hand: quotes are typically guaranteed for 10 contracts a side, so enter orders of at most 10 contracts at a time.
principles.quote: enter orders of a maximum of 10 contracts at a time

rule.notes: Split orders > 10 contracts into ≤10-lot child orders.

principles.principle: Keep trades secret—telling others pressures your ego and makes it harder to take losses.
principles.quote: Don’t tell anyone what you are doing, including your wife or husband.

rule.notes: Behavioral.

principles.chapter: Don't Try to Catch a Falling Knife!
principles.principle: Don't catch a falling knife: don't write puts into a major downtrend and don't buck strong momentum; naked writers should run for cover when the underlying moves against them.
principles.quote: Don’t write puts in the face of a major downtrend.

rule.notes: Block new short puts / bull put spreads when underlying is in a major downtrend.

principles.principle: Only buy options with 'fun money'—capital you are willing to lose entirely—set aside each year.
principles.quote: When you buy options, set aside some fun money every year and kiss it good-bye.

rule.notes: Track annual speculative budget; see Secret 94 for 5–10% cap.

principles.principle: Know when to fold: exit when a trade goes bad, when you're uncomfortable, or when the underlying trend goes against you; taking losses is a virtue.
principles.quote: When the trend of the underlying goes against you, get out!

rule.notes: Exit triggers: adverse trend, discomfort, trade failure.

principles.principle: Ignore sunk cost: decide whether you'd buy the position at today's price; if not, sell.
principles.quote: “Would I buy at today’s price?”

rule.notes: Re-evaluate positions at current price/fair value irrespective of entry cost; if current analysis wouldn't justify entry, recommend exit.

principles.chapter: Always Use Stop-Losses, and Don't Look Back
principles.principle: Always use stop-losses for both buying and writing; they are a MUST for naked writers and credit spread traders.
principles.quote: Stop losses are a MUST for naked writers and credit spread traders.

rule.notes: Require stop for all positions; hard-block shorts/credit spreads without stops.

principles.chapter: Always Use Stop-Losses, and Don't Look Back
principles.principle: Prefer contingency stops based on the underlying's price; if stops use option prices, use bid/ask, not last trade.
principles.quote: make sure to use the option bid or asked price, not the last price

rule.notes: Stop engine: trigger on underlying price; option-based stops must use bid (long exit) / ask (short exit).

principles.chapter: Always Use Stop-Losses, and Don't Look Back
principles.principle: Trailing stop: keep it about 5% from the underlying and adjust as it moves in your favor; take profits on touch.
principles.quote: keeping it 5% away from the stock or futures price

rule.notes: Same as OTS-022-a.

principles.chapter: Always Use Stop-Losses, and Don't Look Back
principles.principle: Always obey stops, especially on writing positions; don't second-guess after being stopped out or taking profits.
principles.quote: Always obey your stop-loss point, especially when it comes to option writing positions.

rule.notes: No overriding/moving stops away on shorts.

principles.principle: Review your track record at least once a year and write down guidelines from your mistakes.
principles.quote: review your track record at least once a year

rule.notes: Annual performance review report.

principles.chapter: The Dragon That You See Is Not the Dragon That Will Burn You
principles.principle: Be prepared for the unexpected: surprise volatility is the buyer's friend and writer's enemy; the next shock comes from an unexpected direction.
principles.quote: Such volatility is the friend of the option buyer but the enemy of the option writer.

rule.notes: Stress test shorts for gaps.

principles.principle: Use internet research and web-based scanners as part of homework.
principles.quote: To gain the edge, you must do your homework

rule.notes: Qualitative.

principles.principle: Avoid analysis paralysis: concentrate on delta, probability of hitting target, implied and historical volatility, and theoretical value; don't treat numbers as set in stone.
principles.quote: concentrate on the delta, probability of hitting your target, implied and historical volatility, and theoretical value

rule.notes: Core metric set for UI.

principles.chapter: How to Use Option Advisory Services
principles.principle: When using advisory recommendations, counter the crowd: use a different option or enter later, take profits before the recommended price, set stops further out, never chase unless still underpriced.
principles.quote: Never chase after an option recommendation unless the option continues to be underpriced.

rule.notes: For externally sourced ideas, only enter if still undervalued; adjust targets/stops away from crowd levels.

principles.chapter: How to Use Option Advisory Services
principles.principle: The option price is the most important aspect of any play; if you can't get your price, wait or pass.
principles.quote: If you can’t get your price, wait till you can or pass.

rule.notes: Don't raise limit beyond value-justified price.

principles.principle: Write a game plan for each position (max risk, profit potential, stops, goals) and an overall plan of how many and what kinds of trades each month/year; ensure each has an edge and realistic objectives.
principles.quote: you need a well defined game plan of each position you enter, written down in black and white

rule.notes: Require plan fields: max risk, profit target, stop, time limit, edge rationale.

principles.principle: Magic Pyramid: at the peak, cheap home-run option buying with fun money—never more than 5%–10% of the portfolio.
principles.quote: never use more than 5%–10% of your portfolio to do so

rule.notes: Total capital in speculative cheap-option buying ≤ 5–10% of total portfolio (warn above 5%, block above 10%).

principles.principle: Asset allocation pyramid: large cash base, then high-rated short/intermediate bonds, 5–10% hard assets, stocks/funds (with options for income, acquisition and insurance), then aggressive spreads/naked writing, then speculative buying at the top.
principles.quote: About 5% to 10% of your portfolio should be in hard assets

value.stocks: with covered calls/put writing/put insurance/LEAPS spreads

rule.notes: Portfolio framework.

principles.chapter: Thar Is Gold in Them Thar Hills
principles.principle: The most powerful strategy is buying cheap, undervalued options (especially puts), exploiting fat-tailed surprise volatility.
principles.quote: the most powerful of all option strategies is to just BUY CHEAP OPTIONS, especially puts

rule.notes: Core strategy for speculative sleeve.

principles.chapter: Thar Is Gold in Them Thar Hills
principles.principle: Buying procedure: scan for undervalued options; check charts for no heavy overhead resistance (calls) or support beneath (puts) and that the underlying has made the needed move before in the time frame; check IV and HV are at a low ebb; run probability analysis.
principles.quote: to make sure these volatilities are at a low ebb on the charts

rule.notes: Full long-option screening pipeline.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Stock option buying rules: buy only underpriced options.
principles.quote: 1. Buy only underpriced options.

rule.notes: Long price < fair value.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Buy cheap stock options—priced under 1, or under 2.5 for LEAPS.
principles.quote: Buy cheap options—options priced under 1 or under 2.5 for Leaps.

rule.notes: Stock option premium < 1.00; LEAPS < 2.50 (per share).

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Buy close-to-the-money options where the stock has a good chance to move across the strike.
principles.quote: 3. Buy close-to-the-money options.

rule.notes: Prefer strikes near spot; require realistic chance of crossing strike. No % OTM limit given.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Buy options with as much time as possible before expiration.
principles.quote: 4. Buy options with as much time as possible before expiration.

rule.notes: Rank by more DTE (subject to price and value).

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Buy options where the underlying has potential for increased future volatility.
principles.quote: Buy options where the underlying stock has the potential for increased volatility in the future.

rule.notes: Prefer low current IV/HV vs history, event-prone names.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Put the same number of dollars in each long-option position.
principles.quote: 6. Put the same number of dollars in each position.

rule.notes: Equal-dollar sizing across long-option positions.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Diversify option buying over time—over 2 years.
principles.quote: 7. Diversify over time (2 years).

rule.notes: Pace option-buying entries across a 2-year horizon.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Buy in quantity to save commissions.
principles.quote: 8. Buy in quantity to save commissions.

rule.notes: Balance with min 3 contracts (Secret 25) and ≤10 per order (Secret 81).

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Try to buy options with at least a 20% chance of profit (stock and commodity options).
principles.quote: Try to buy options where there is at least a 20% chance of profit.

rule.notes: Long option P(profit) ≥ 20%.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Option Buying
principles.principle: Commodity option buying: buy only underpriced, close-to-the-money options with maximum time, volatility potential, chance to cross strike, ≥20% probability, diversify over 2 years, and pay no more than $400 per option.
principles.quote: 2. Do not pay more than $400 for an option.

rule.notes: Futures option premium ≤ $400 per contract.

principles.principle: Prefer index credit spreads over naked stock writing: indexes dampen single-stock surprise volatility and spreads cap risk and margin.
principles.quote: A powerful play is the INDEX CREDIT SPREAD.

rule.notes: For writing, recommend broad-based index credit spreads over naked stock options.

principles.principle: Credit spread risk is the strike width less the credit; the wider the spread, the greater the risk.
principles.quote: The wider the spread, the greater the risk.

rule.notes: Display max loss = (width − credit) × 100.

principles.principle: Set the credit spread stop-loss out-of-the-money, away from the short strike (e.g., short OEX 400 call → stop about 395).
principles.quote: I always set my stop-loss out-of-the-money and away from the strike price of the option I am writing.

rule.notes: Call credit spread: stop below short strike; put credit spread: stop above short strike (example: ~5 points on OEX).

principles.principle: Pass on a credit spread if the simulated probability of hitting the stop-loss during the life of the option exceeds 20%.
principles.quote: If the probability is greater than 20% of hitting the stop-loss during the life of the option, I pass.

rule.notes: Block index credit spread if simulated P(touch stop) > 20%.

principles.principle: Never buck the market trend—never enter put credit spreads in the teeth of a decline.
principles.quote: Never will I enter put spreads in the teeth of a decline.

rule.notes: Block bull put spreads during market declines.

principles.principle: Take profits and close a credit spread when it narrows and generates a good profit; also exit if the trend turns against you or you get uncomfortable.
principles.quote: make sure to take profits and close out your position if the spread narrows and generates a good profit during the life of the trade

rule.notes: 'Good profit' not quantified; configurable. Also exit on adverse trend.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Index Credit Spreads
principles.principle: Index credit spread rules: use index options; sell a far-out-of-the-money option; buy one 5, 10 or 15 points further out.
principles.quote: Buy an index option that is 5, 10, or 15 points further out-of-the-money.

rule.notes: Underlying must be an index; short leg far OTM; width ∈ {5,10,15} index points.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Index Credit Spreads
principles.principle: Index credit spread: get a credit of at least .45.
principles.quote: 4. Make certain to get a credit of at least .45.

rule.notes: Net credit ≥ 0.45 per share ($45/spread).

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Index Credit Spreads
principles.principle: Index credit spread: enter with less than three weeks before expiration.
principles.quote: 5. Enter such spreads with less than three weeks before expiration.

rule.notes: DTE < 21 calendar days at entry.

principles.chapter: Rules of the Road for Index Credit Spreads
principles.principle: Index credit spread: set an out-of-the-money stop with an 85% chance of not being touched.
principles.quote: 7. Set a stop-loss where there is an 85% chance of not touching the stop-loss.

rule.notes: Stop placement: P(not touch) ≥ 85% (compare Secret 97: pass if P(touch) > 20%; Secret 97 example had 96%).

principles.principle: Ratio hedge: own the stock and write more overpriced long-term calls than shares covered (e.g., 2 calls per 100 shares); involves naked risk—only for traders who tolerate it; key is finding overpriced options.
principles.quote: The key to success here is to find some overpriced options.

rule.notes: Requires overvalued short options; upside stop at the upper breakeven (example: 0–50 range on Rambus).

principles.principle: Use a simulator to estimate the probability of hitting the ratio hedge's stop-loss points (example: 4% probability, 96% chance of breakeven or better).
principles.quote: your probability of hitting 50 would have been 4%, so there is a 96% chance of breaking even or making a profit

rule.notes: Compute P(touch) of upper/lower breakeven stops. No explicit threshold given for ratio hedges.

principles.principle: Diagonal credit spread: write a near-term OTM option and buy a further-out-strike, longer-term option, only for a credit (or at most a very small debit); use a stop to avoid going in-the-money on the short.
principles.quote: However, I only do trades where there is a credit.

rule.notes: Diagonal net price must be a credit (or at worst very small debit).

principles.principle: Diagonal rules: short strike about 3 to 5+ points OTM; long option expires 1+ month after the short with strike 2.5–5 points beyond the short; short option under 2 months to expiration.
principles.quote: Try to select a spread where the option you are writing has less than 2 months before expiration.

rule.notes: Structure validation for diagonal spreads; prefer 5-point spreads and long leg as far out in time as possible.

principles.principle: Diagonal stop: slightly in-the-money of the short strike (e.g., 55 call → stop 56); exit when stop hits, at short expiration, or when the short loses most of its value; can keep the long as a free option.
principles.quote: Set a stop-loss that is slightly in-the-money of the option that you have sold (i.e. a 55 call would have a stop at 56).

rule.notes: Use simulator to confirm low P(touch stop). Book's track record: 15/18 (83%) profitable in 2002.

principles.chapter: The Ultimate Power Play: The Secret Surrogate
principles.principle: Long-term (LEAPS) debit spreads are powerful stock surrogates with potential payoffs up to 1000%.
principles.quote: It is a debit Leaps® spread or long term option debit spread.

rule.notes: Preferred bullish stock-surrogate structure.

principles.chapter: The Ultimate Power Play: The Secret Surrogate
principles.principle: LEAPS debit spread design: short strike several strikes away—10 points or more between strikes—and maximum profit of at least 400%.
principles.quote: Try to design one that has a spread of 10 points or more between strike prices and shows a maximum profit of at least 400%.

rule.notes: Width ≥ 10 points; (width − debit)/debit ≥ 4.0.

principles.chapter: The Ultimate Power Play: The Secret Surrogate
principles.principle: LEAPS debit spread: use a simulator to find one with over an 80% chance of profiting (examples: 80% chance of doubling during life).
principles.quote: using a simulator, try to find one that has over an 80% chance of profiting

rule.notes: Simulated P(profit at some time during life) > 80%.

principles.chapter: The Ultimate Power Play: The Secret Surrogate
principles.principle: Take profits on half of a LEAPS debit spread if it doubles; let the rest ride with a trailing stop.
principles.quote: Take profits on half of your position if the spread price doubles in value.

rule.notes: Sell 50% at 2x; trailing stop on remainder.

principles.principle: Liquidity (daily volume and open interest) matters: deep ITM/far OTM options may have none, and options with 7–9 months left normally lack the liquidity of 2–3 month options.
principles.quote: options that usually have lives of seven, eight, or nine months normally do not have the liquidity that an option of two or three months would maintain

rule.notes: Check average daily volume and open interest; warn on illiquid strikes/expirations. No numeric minimum given.

principles.principle: Option price = intrinsic value + time value; time value declines to zero at expiration; experienced players mostly trade OTM options (time value only).
principles.quote: INTRINSIC VALUE + TIME VALUE = OPTION PRICE

rule.notes: Display intrinsic and time value.

principles.principle: Debit spread math: cost = long − short price = max risk; max gain = strike width − cost; evaluate max % return and probability of profit/max return.
principles.quote: The result is the cost of the spread and your maximum risk.

rule.notes: Tutorial; short leg OTM by 2.5, 5, 10 or more points.

principles.principle: Credit spread math: credit = short − long price; max risk = strike width − credit.
principles.quote: Your maximum risk is the difference between the strike prices

rule.notes: Tutorial.
